## Nx Affected Builds Overview

Using nx affected is a powerful tool to reduce the amount of compute that needs to be run. This builds only the projects affected by your changes, saving significant time in CI/CD pipelines.

## How the Dependency Graph Works

Thanks to its smart dependency graph analysis, Nx can trace dependencies used by different projects and can therefore avoid unnecessary cache misses even when a root level lockfile changes. To be able to compute the affected projects, Nx will generate an Affected Graph with all affected projects and their dependencies.

By passing the PR's target branch as the base argument to nx affected commands, Nx will figure out what has changed. Then, based on the dependency graph, it automatically runs the tasks for only the affected projects.

## CI Strategy Best Practices

The recommended approach is to set the base SHA to the latest successful commit on the main branch. This ensures that all changes since the last successful CI run are accounted for.

Nx works with all major CI/CD systems. It provides specific integrations for GitHub Actions, CircleCI, and others to optimize build times using its caching features.

## Key Optimization Considerations

Ensure your Named Inputs are correctly configured. Named inputs define if modifying a file can impact the output of a target. For example, modifying a spec file can impact the test but not the build.

If too many projects are affected with each modification, ensure the split of your apps/libs is correctly done. Often, shared libraries are used for many projects with utilities needed by only one project. In such cases, touching that library affects all projects.

Here is a comprehensive overview of **Monorepo CI/CD Dependency-Based Build Triggering Best Practices (2024–2025)**:

---

## 🏗️ Core Principle: Build Only What Changed

A naive pipeline that rebuilds everything on every commit will quickly become a bottleneck. The foundational best practice is **selective, dependency-aware builds**:

- To avoid unnecessary builds, configure your CI system to trigger builds only for affected projects. Tools like Bazel, Gradle, and Buck can analyze the dependency graph to determine what needs to be rebuilt based on changes.
- Selective builds and tests allow the CI/CD pipeline to detect changes and execute tasks only on the affected projects. This approach reduces the time and resources required for each pipeline run.

---

## 🔀 Strategy 1: Path-Based Triggering

Use path-based triggers in your CI/CD pipelines to run jobs only when specific parts of the codebase change. For example, GitHub Actions supports path filtering to trigger workflows based on file changes.

**GitLab CI** also supports this natively: In GitLab 16.4, the `include` with `rules:changes` for pipelines was introduced. Previously, you could include with `rules:if`, but not `rules:changes`, making this update extremely powerful. Now, you can simply use the `include` keyword and define the monorepo rules in your project pipeline configuration.

Ideally, you can completely decouple the pipelines and only run each pipeline based on changes to that specific application's source code.

---

## 🔗 Strategy 2: Dependency Graph Analysis

Dependency graphs help identify relationships between projects in a monorepo. By visualizing dependencies, developers can understand how changes impact other projects and configure pipelines accordingly. Tools like Nx and Bazel generate dependency graphs, which CI/CD pipelines can use to determine which parts of the monorepo need building and testing. Dependency graphs allow the pipeline to prioritize builds for high-impact components, making the entire workflow more efficient.

---

## 🛠️ Strategy 3: Modular Pipelines Per Project

For complex monorepos, modularizing CI/CD pipelines can simplify configuration and improve flexibility. Modular pipelines divide tasks based on projects, enabling each project to have its own set of build, test, and deployment stages. This structure allows teams to scale and adjust workflows as the codebase grows. For example, one pipeline module could handle frontend builds, while another focuses on backend services.

---

## ⚡ Strategy 4: Intelligent Caching

Caching is essential for optimizing CI/CD pipelines in monorepos. Caching allows the pipeline to reuse previously built artifacts, avoiding redundant work and speeding up builds.

Many CI/CD platforms also integrate with monorepo tooling to leverage remote caching and affected-project detection, ensuring that pipelines rebuild and test only what has actually changed.

---

## 🧰 Key Tools in 2024–2025

| Tool | Strength |
|------|----------|
| **Nx** | An extensible build system with first-class support for JavaScript and TypeScript, offering deep architectural awareness, code generation, and powerful caching capabilities. Nx understands the relationships between projects in your monorepo and can selectively rebuild only what has changed. |
| **Turborepo** | Focuses on high-performance task running with aggressive caching. Its minimalist philosophy emphasizes speed and simplicity, making it an excellent choice for teams that want fast builds without extensive configuration. |
| **Bazel / Pants** | Specialized monorepo engines that provide first-class support for dependency graphs, incremental builds, and hermetic caching; they often require upfront engineering to standardize builds. |

---

## 🏆 Evaluation Criteria for Tooling

When evaluating tools, prioritize these capabilities: incremental orchestration, remote cache/artifact storage, parallel execution, fine-grained permissions, and metrics/observability. Also check integrations with deployment targets and secrets managers, and consider the ecosystem for language support.

---

## 🚀 Parallel Execution

Optimize your CI/CD pipelines by running tests and builds in parallel where possible. This approach reduces build times and improves efficiency.

---

## 🔐 Ownership & Governance

Best practices include modular project structure, strict code ownership rules, dependency graphs to isolate changes, and using selective build/test pipelines to avoid slow full builds.

Implement access controls using tools like GitHub's CODEOWNERS file to manage who can approve changes to specific parts of the repository.

---

## ☁️ Deployment Patterns

Deploy individual services independently within the monorepo. Containerization allows for separate deployment and testing of microservices. Implement deployment strategies like blue-green or canary deployments to minimize downtime and risk.

---

## 📌 Summary

Monorepo CI/CD is rapidly becoming a default strategy for large engineering organizations that need to manage multiple projects and shared libraries from a single repository. When done well, monorepo CI/CD reduces integration friction, improves code reuse, and enables cross-project refactors with confidence. However, monorepos also introduce unique challenges around build scale, pipeline cost, and developer velocity, so designing an effective CI/CD system requires careful trade-offs and operational know-how.

The winning formula is: **path/change detection + dependency graph traversal + intelligent caching + parallel execution + modular pipelines**.

Bazel can dramatically reduce build and test times on each pull request by integrating caching strategies into CI workflows, with persistent caching meaning CI workers start from a known good state, only re-building and re-testing what's necessary.

## GitLab CI `changes` Keyword and Transitive Dependencies

The `changes` keyword can be used to run jobs only when specific files change. However, there's an important limitation regarding transitive dependencies in monorepo setups.

### Manual Listing vs. Automated Approach

The key challenge with the `changes` keyword in monorepos is handling transitive dependencies:

The GitLab CI/CD `changes` keyword is limited to wildcard paths. This means you cannot automatically detect when a shared dependency (like a shared library or package) changes and needs to trigger builds for all consuming services.

A workaround is to explicitly add all transitive dependencies to `needs:`, however this may not be realistic as it adds a lot of bloat and complexity to the YAML files and there's also a limit on how many `needs:` you can have on any one job.

### Automated Alternative Using Dependency Tools

Some teams use tools like turborepo that plug directly into the dependencies defined in each package.json to trigger builds, which breaks free from the GitLab CI/CD `changes` keyword where they are limited to wildcard paths, and they add a call to `turbo-ignore` for each app to determine if they should include jobs for that app in the pipeline.yml file.

In summary, GitLab's `changes` keyword requires **manual listing** of paths to monitor, while more advanced approaches use external dependency analysis tools to **automatically detect** transitive dependencies.

# GitLab CI Monorepo Handling

GitLab CI manages monorepo builds through conditional pipeline inclusion and the `changes` keyword, which has evolved significantly.

## The Modern Approach

As of GitLab 16.4, the platform supports `include` with `rules:changes` for pipelines. This allows developers to conditionally include application-specific pipeline files based on directory modifications. Rather than extending hidden jobs repeatedly across configuration files, engineers can now define monorepo rules directly in the project-level `.gitlab-ci.yml`.

## How Changes Detection Works

The `changes` rule evaluates which files have been modified and triggers corresponding pipelines. For example:

> "include: - local: '/java/j.gitlab-ci.yml' rules: - changes: - 'java/*'"

This configuration ensures the Java pipeline only loads when the `java/` directory is updated.

## Important Caveat

There's a notable behavior to understand: the `changes` rule always evaluates as true when pushing a new branch or tag, meaning all included jobs run on initial branch creation regardless of directory modifications. GitLab recommends creating feature branches first, then opening merge requests to avoid this behavior.

This approach eliminates code redundancy and reduces human error compared to earlier workarounds that required extending hidden jobs across multiple configuration files.

# Monorepo CI Best Practices: Key Strategies and Trade-offs

## Dependency-Based Build Triggering

The article emphasizes **selective builds** as the cornerstone approach. Rather than rebuilding entire monorepos, teams should "only execute jobs relevant to changed libraries and their dependents."

Two implementation patterns emerge:

1. **Path-based filtering** (GitHub Actions): Predefined workflows trigger based on file changes
2. **Dynamic pipeline generation** (Buildkite): Runtime calculation of affected components enables more sophisticated dependency awareness

Modern build tools like Bazel, Gradle, and Buck natively understand dependency graphs, caching results to skip unchanged components.

## Critical Trade-offs

| Strategy | Benefits | Costs |
|----------|----------|----
| **Shallow clones/sparse checkouts** | Faster performance, reduced bandwidth | Limited history; potential build failures from missing context |
| **Trunk-based development** | Fewer merge conflicts, natural CI alignment | Requires strong team discipline and robust infrastructure |
| **Merge queues** | Prevents broken builds, serializes safely | Adds complexity; potential merge delays |

## Essential Practices

The framework prioritizes: centralized dependency management, CODEOWNERS for access control, and feature flags for in-progress work. The article stresses that "a monorepo won't automatically solve organizational problems"—success demands deliberate architectural decisions and consistent enforcement.

The article identifies a significant issue: "A job with needs keyword is run even if needed job is skipped." To work around this problem, the author recommends **explicitly adding all transitive dependencies to the `needs:` field**. This ensures that deployment jobs don't proceed when upstream tasks fail or are skipped.

GitLab implements the `only:changes` feature to selectively trigger pipelines based on modified files. This allows developers to run only affected component pipelines rather than the entire monorepo suite.

The key limitation noted: "the limit of jobs you can have in `needs:` is 5." This constraint forces teams to restructure dependencies by moving dependent jobs upstream—a workaround that sacrifices architectural clarity for pragmatic execution.

## Practical Trade-offs

The author suggests these limitations will likely improve as the DAG feature matures, but currently require balancing pipeline accuracy against maintainability in larger monorepos.

# Gradle Monorepo Affected Modules Discussion

## Issue Summary

A developer requested native Gradle support for building and deploying only affected modules in a monorepo, similar to NX's `affected` command for frontend projects.

## Proposed Solutions

**Community Workaround:**
One responder provided a Kotlin-based solution using `addTransitiveConsumersTask()` to create custom tasks that identify and build modules affected by dependencies. This approach "will run the check task for some-library and all projects in the repo that consume it directly or transitively."

**Official Position:**
Gradle maintainers declined to implement this feature, stating: "For building code, the Gradle story is based on remote caching, configuration cache, and UP-TO-DATE checks." They noted Gradle lacks specific deployment support since core deploy tasks are never up-to-date.

## Actual Resolution

The issue creator eventually resolved their need using NX directly, despite the additional Node.js dependency, finding it "works perfectly" for their use case.

Based on the search results, here's a comprehensive overview of the trade-offs between path-based filtering and dependency graph detection in monorepos:

## Path-Based Filtering

**Pros:**
- Simple to implement ("only run tests if files in /backend changed")
- Lower computational overhead for detecting what changed
- Straightforward to understand and maintain

**Cons:**
- Requires maintaining a complex web of dependencies
- Can trigger false positives (e.g., running tests when you don't need to)
- Limited accuracy with implicit dependencies across the codebase
- Dependencies are not always explicit or detectable through functional tests

## Dependency Graph Detection

**Pros:**
- Smart dependency graph analysis can trace dependencies used by different projects and avoid unnecessary cache misses
- Provides task orchestration, intelligent caching, and dependency graph analysis that significantly reduce CI/CD times. Nx understands the relationships between projects and can selectively rebuild only what has changed
- More accurate detection of affected projects
- Better support for complex interdependencies

**Cons:**
- Higher upfront computational cost to build and analyze the graph
- Requires more sophisticated tooling
- Without proper tooling, build consistency, and version enforcement, a monorepo can become chaotic. Tools like Nx or Turborepo help, but require configuration and team buy-in

## Key Trade-off
The fundamental trade-off is **simplicity vs. accuracy**: path-based filtering is easier to implement but less precise, while dependency graph detection requires more investment in tooling but provides significantly better performance and reliability at scale.

Based on the search results, I've found detailed information about GitLab CI's `changes` keyword behavior and workarounds for monorepos:

## Key Finding: The "Always True" Behavior

The changes rule always evaluates to true when pushing a new branch or a new tag to GitLab, so all jobs included will run upon first push to a branch regardless of the rules:changes definition.

## Monorepo Limitation

This behavior creates a challenge for monorepos where you want to run jobs only when specific parts of the repository change.

## Workarounds

**Official GitLab Approach (GitLab 16.4+):**
In GitLab 16.4, GitLab introduced include with rules:changes for pipelines. Previously, you could include with rules:if, but not rules:changes. Now, you can simply use the include keyword and define the monorepo rules in your project pipeline configuration.

**Practical Workaround:**
You can mitigate this experience by creating your feature branch first and then opening a merge request to begin your development, since the first push to the branch when it is created will force all jobs to run.

**Alternative Solution:**
For more complex scenarios, some teams use custom tooling. One approach involves adding a custom component that acts as a webhook endpoint which triggers the pipeline explicitly via API, parsing which paths changed and setting variables accordingly.

**Dependency-Based Approach:**
Tools like turborepo's turbo-ignore command can plug into package.json dependencies to determine whether to trigger builds, breaking free from the GitLab CI/CD changes keyword limitation to wildcard paths.

# Monorepo CI/CD Dependency-Based Build Triggering: Best Practices Research

## 1. Is It Best Practice to Rebuild a Service When Its Dependency Modules Change?

**Yes, absolutely.** This is the foundational principle of modern monorepo CI/CD. Failing to trigger builds when shared dependency modules change leads to "dependency blindness" — deploying a service that looks unchanged but may be broken by changes in a library it depends on.

Your current project already implements this correctly. For example, `search-api` declares `shared/**/*`, `domain/search/**/*`, `outbound-adapter/search/**/*`, etc. in its `changes:` list. This is intentional and correct — not accidental over-specification.

---

## 2. How Major Companies and Tools Handle This

### Google / Bazel

Bazel models builds as a **Directed Acyclic Graph (DAG) of targets**, not files. Each `BUILD` file explicitly declares what a target depends on. When computing what to rebuild for a given change:

- Bazel uses `bazel query` to determine the transitive reverse dependency closure: "which targets need this target as an input?"
- Google's CI system runs only tests in the affected set, even for third-party library updates, because those updates change the graph too.
- The community tool [`bazel-diff`](https://github.com/Tinder/bazel-diff) (by Tinder) allows computing the exact affected set between two git revisions.

Bazel's key strength: dependency tracking is **at the target level** (not file level), enabling maximum precision. The cost is that every BUILD file must be manually maintained.

### Nx (JavaScript/TypeScript ecosystem, but also has Gradle plugin)

Nx uses an automated **project graph** built by analyzing `package.json` dependencies (or Gradle module dependencies via `@nx/gradle`). The `nx affected` command:

1. Identifies changed files between the current HEAD and a base SHA (usually the last successful CI commit).
2. Walks the project graph to find all projects that transitively depend on any changed project.
3. Runs tasks only for those projects.

```bash
# In CI: only run builds/tests for projects affected by this PR
npx nx affected --target=build --base=origin/main
```

Nx also supports **Named Inputs** — allowing you to specify that changing a `*.spec.ts` file only affects `test` targets, not `build` targets. This avoids unnecessary rebuilds.

Importantly, Nx's `@nx/gradle` plugin reflects Gradle's `settings.gradle.kts` dependency graph into Nx's project graph automatically.

### Turborepo (Vercel, primarily Node.js)

Turborepo builds a task dependency graph from `package.json` workspaces. The `--affected` flag (added relatively recently) runs tasks only for packages with changes and their dependents. `turbo-ignore` is a companion tool used in CI to detect whether a specific app or any of its dependencies changed.

Key limitation: Turborepo had documented issues with dependency graph accuracy in some edge cases (see [GitHub issue #9234](https://github.com/vercel/turborepo/issues/9234)).

### GitLab CI `changes:` Keyword

GitLab's approach is **path-based filtering** — purely at the file system level, not the semantic dependency level.

**How it works:**
- On MR events: compares changed files in the MR against the `changes:` path list.
- On push events: compares the pushed commit(s) against the previous state.
- Since **GitLab 16.4**: `include:` with `rules: changes:` is supported, allowing conditional inclusion of sub-pipeline files.

**Known limitation — the "always true" branch behavior:**
When a new branch is first pushed, `changes:` always evaluates to `true` because there is no previous state to compare against. All jobs run. This is a [known open issue](https://gitlab.com/gitlab-org/gitlab/-/issues/293645) and is by design for safety. The practical workaround is to create the branch first (empty push), then open the MR.

**GitLab cannot detect transitive dependencies automatically.** The `changes:` keyword only understands glob path patterns. If `domain/search/` is changed and `search-api` depends on it, you must explicitly list `domain/search/**/*` in `search-api`'s changes list — which is exactly what your project does.

---

## 3. Common Strategies and Comparison

| Strategy | Description | Tools |
|----------|-------------|-------|
| **Path-based filtering** | Explicitly list all paths (including dependency paths) that should trigger a given service build | GitLab `changes:`, GitHub Actions `paths:` |
| **Dependency graph-based** | Automatically compute affected set from the project dependency graph | Nx, Bazel, Turborepo, DoorDash custom tooling |
| **Build everything always** | Every commit triggers a full build/test of all services | Simple but doesn't scale |

---

## 4. Trade-offs of Each Approach

### Path-Based Filtering (your current approach in GitLab CI)

**Pros:**
- Simple to understand — the CI YAML is fully explicit and auditable
- No additional tooling required beyond GitLab CI itself
- Works well when the dependency graph is relatively stable
- Zero overhead: no graph computation at CI trigger time
- GitLab-native: no external orchestration layer needed

**Cons:**
- **Must be manually maintained.** When you add a new shared module (e.g., a new `outbound/client/` module that `search-api` depends on), you must remember to add that path to `search_api_changes`. This is a maintenance burden and a **source of bugs** — it's easy to forget, leading to a service that should have been rebuilt getting missed.
- **No transitive detection.** If `shared/` depends on some `proto/` definition, and you change `proto/`, your `changes:` lists must explicitly include both `proto/**/*` and `shared/**/*`.
- **Cannot express semantic dependency rules.** You can't say "only trigger `test` but not `build` if only a `*Test.kt` file changed."
- Possible **false positives**: listing `shared/**/*` means even a README change in shared triggers a rebuild.

### Dependency Graph-Based (Nx, Bazel, Turborepo)

**Pros:**
- **Automatically correct:** adding a new dependency in `build.gradle.kts` is all that's needed for CI to pick it up
- **Precise:** the affected set is computed from the actual dependency graph, not manually curated path lists
- **Supports transitive dependencies** automatically
- Can express more nuanced rules (e.g., "test files only affect test targets")
- DoorDash (Kotlin/Gradle monorepo with 330+ Gradle projects) used this approach with custom tooling: they scan all `settings.gradle` files to build a reverse dependency graph, then compute affected targets for each change.

**Cons:**
- Requires additional tooling (Nx, Bazel, or custom scripts)
- Higher setup cost and learning curve
- For Gradle specifically, there is **no native "affected" command** built into Gradle itself. The [Gradle team declined to implement it](https://github.com/gradle/gradle/issues/20705), suggesting their story is based on remote caching instead.
- Adds complexity to the CI pipeline

### Build Everything Always

**Pros:** Simple, always safe — no risk of missing a rebuild.

**Cons:** Completely unscalable. For a project with 15+ modules like yours, a change to `domain/keyword` would rebuild and retest everything including unrelated services on every commit. Wasted CI minutes and slow feedback loops.

---

## 5. Your Project's Current Approach: Analysis

Your project uses **path-based filtering with manually curated changes lists** in YAML anchors (`&search_api_changes`, `&dynamic_indexer_changes`). Here's how it looks:

```yaml
# bootstrap/search-api/.gitlab/.gitlab-ci.yml
.search_api_changes: &search_api_changes
  - .gitlab-ci.yml
  - .gitlab/**/*
  - bootstrap/search-api/**/*
  - proto/**/*
  - shared/**/*
  - domain/search/**/*
  - domain/keyword/**/*
  - application/search/**/*
  - inbound-adapter/rest-api/**/*
  - outbound-adapter/keyword/**/*
  - outbound-adapter/search/**/*
  - outbound/client/keyword-analyzer/**/*
  - outbound/repository/cache/**/*
  - outbound/repository/elasticsearch/common/**/*
  - outbound/repository/elasticsearch/backoffice/**/*
  - outbound/repository/elasticsearch/front/**/*
```

**This is the industry-standard approach for GitLab CI with a Gradle-based monorepo.** The major companies that use Nx/Bazel do so with JavaScript/TypeScript (Nx) or have invested heavily in custom build infrastructure (Google, DoorDash). For a Kotlin/Spring Boot project on GitLab CI without a dedicated platform engineering team, manually curated `changes:` lists with YAML anchors is the pragmatic best practice.

The key risks to watch for:
1. **Forgetting to update `changes:` lists when new modules are added.** For example, if you add a new `outbound/client/proxy-api` module that `dynamic-indexer` depends on but forget to add `outbound/client/proxy-api/**/*` to `dynamic_indexer_changes`, CI will miss it.
2. The CI files themselves (`.gitlab-ci.yml`, `.gitlab/**/*`) are included in both lists — this is a good safety measure ensuring that CI config changes always trigger a full rebuild.

---

## 6. Well-Known References and Documentation

**GitLab CI Monorepo:**
- [Building a GitLab CI/CD pipeline for a monorepo the easy way (GitLab Blog, 2024)](https://about.gitlab.com/blog/2024/07/30/building-a-gitlab-ci-cd-pipeline-for-a-monorepo-the-easy-way/)
- [5 Tips for managing monorepos in GitLab (GitLab Blog)](https://about.gitlab.com/blog/2022/07/12/tips-for-managing-monorepos-in-gitlab/)
- [Improving monorepo performance — GitLab Docs](https://docs.gitlab.com/user/project/repository/monorepos/)
- [GitLab Monorepo Pipelines — Aaron's Blog](https://aarongorka.com/blog/gitlab-monorepo-pipelines/) — detailed analysis of `changes:` + DAG + `needs:` interactions
- [GitLab `changes:` "always true" on new branch — GitLab Issue #293645](https://gitlab.com/gitlab-org/gitlab/-/issues/293645)

**Nx (dependency graph-based):**
- [Run Only Tasks Affected by a PR — Nx Docs](https://nx.dev/docs/features/ci-features/affected)
- [Deep Dive into Nx Affected — smartsdlc.dev](https://smartsdlc.dev/blog/deep-dive-into-nx-affected/)
- [Nx Gradle Tutorial](https://nx.dev/docs/getting-started/tutorials/gradle-tutorial)
- [Improving monorepo build times using Nx — BlackRock Engineering](https://engineering.blackrock.com/improving-monorepo-build-times-using-nx-890774863677)

**Bazel:**
- [Dependencies — Bazel Docs](https://bazel.build/concepts/dependencies)
- [Building a Monorepo with Bazel — Earthly Blog](https://earthly.dev/blog/monorepo-with-bazel/)
- [Overcoming monorepo challenges with Bazel — VirtusLab](https://virtuslab.com/blog/backend/overcoming-monorepo-challenges/)
- [Solving Monorepo Hell with Bazel — Medium](https://medium.com/@erfan.mohebi/solving-monorepo-hell-with-bazel-a-deep-dive-into-modern-build-systems-f70c831bb227)

**Gradle Monorepo:**
- [Only build and deploy affected modules in a Gradle Monorepo — Gradle Issue #20705](https://github.com/gradle/gradle/issues/20705) — Gradle team declined native "affected" support; use remote caching instead
- [Building a Gradle-Based Monorepo for Kotlin Backends — DPE Summit 2025](https://dpe.org/sessions/ashwin-kachhara/building-a-gradle-based-monorepo-for-kotlin-backends/)

**General Monorepo CI Best Practices:**
- [Monorepo CI Best Practices — Buildkite](https://buildkite.com/resources/blog/monorepo-ci-best-practices/)
- [How to implement CI/CD strategies for monorepos — Graphite](https://graphite.com/guides/implement-cicd-strategies-monorepos)
- [Monorepo Tooling in 2025 — Wisp CMS](https://www.wisp.blog/blog/monorepo-tooling-in-2025-a-comprehensive-guide)
- [Monorepo Tools comparison — monorepo.tools](https://monorepo.tools/)

---

## Summary

Your current approach — **manually curated path-based `changes:` lists in GitLab CI** — is the correct and widely-used pattern for Gradle/Kotlin monorepos on GitLab CI. It directly answers the question: yes, listing dependency module paths in the `changes:` of each service is not redundant; it is required because GitLab CI has no automatic dependency graph awareness.

The primary maintenance discipline required: whenever a new Gradle module is added to the project and it becomes a dependency of `search-api` or `dynamic-indexer`, the corresponding path must be added to `search_api_changes` or `dynamic_indexer_changes` respectively. The alternative (using Nx with `@nx/gradle`) would automate this but adds a Node.js toolchain dependency to a pure JVM project.
